# ValetFS

> A vault whose contents live on the user's phone. A local daemon (`valetfs`)
> holds them in memory only and serves them to this machine while the phone
> allows it. Nothing is written to disk by the daemon.

Repository: https://github.com/winm2m/valet-fs
Install CLI: curl -fsSL https://winm2m.github.io/valet-fs/install.sh | bash
Install Claude Code skill: curl -fsSL https://winm2m.github.io/valet-fs/install-skill.sh | bash

## AI agents: read this first

Never read a secret in order to use it. `valetfs cat` writes the value to
stdout, and from there into your transcript, the shell history, and any log
wrapping you. Use `valetfs exec` so the value goes into the child process
instead:

    valetfs exec fs:/keys/aws.env -- aws s3 ls s3://bucket
    valetfs exec --as EL_KEY fs:/keys/elevenlabs/api-key.txt -- node tts.mjs
    valetfs exec --as-file KEYFILE fs:/keys/apple.p8 -- ./sign.sh

`valetfs ls` and `valetfs status` are safe to call; they report names, sizes and
daemon state, never contents. `valetfs cat` remains for the case where a person
needs to read a value with their own eyes.

If your harness blocks `cat` — Claude Code reports `[Credential
Materialization]` — do not work around it. The default block is correct: an
agent that can drain a vault unprompted defeats the point of a vault. Either use
`exec`, or ask the human to run `valetfs setup-claude` once. An agent cannot run
`setup-claude` on its own behalf; the same classifier blocks editing its own
settings with `[Self-Modification]`.

`exec` will not get you past a child command whose job is to inspect the secret.
`valetfs exec --as V fs:/keys/x -- sh -c 'echo ${#V}'` is blocked as
`[Credential Exploration]`. Use `valetfs ls -l` if you want to confirm a secret
is present and see its size.

## Path rules

Vault paths take an `fs:` prefix: `fs:/keys/aws.env`. A bare `/keys/aws.env` is
a path on this machine. `ls`, `cat` and `exec` reject a host path outright, but
`cp` and `mv` accept one of each and infer the direction — so
`valetfs cp secret.env /keys/x` is a silent local file copy that writes
plaintext outside the vault.

## Commands

    valetfs serve --join <KEY>                 join a session provisioned by the app
    valetfs exec <vault-path>... -- <cmd>      run a command with secrets in its environment
    valetfs status                             daemon state, bytes used, grace countdown
    valetfs ls [-la] fs:/keys                  list vault contents
    valetfs cat fs:/keys/x                     print a secret (for people, not agents)
    valetfs cp|mv|rm|mkdir|rmdir ...           move files in and out of the vault
    valetfs setup-claude [--print]             allow Claude Code to call valetfs unprompted
    valetfs vaults <list|forget|forget-all>    manage accepted vault identities
    valetfs --version

## valetfs exec

    valetfs exec [options] <vault-path>... -- <command> [args...]

    --env <vault-path>           inject every KEY=VALUE from a dotenv file
                                 (a bare positional path means the same)
    --as NAME=<vault-path>       inject the file body as $NAME
    --as NAME <vault-path>       same, path as the next argument
    --as-file NAME=<vault-path>  materialise the file; $NAME holds its path
    --as-file NAME <vault-path>  same, path as the next argument
    --keep-newline               keep the trailing newline on --as values
                                 (trimmed by default, because a key with a
                                 newline glued on fails as an auth header)

Every option repeats, so one command can inject several secrets. The child's
stdout, stderr and exit code pass through unchanged, so `exec` drops into an
existing pipeline or `&&` chain.

`--as-file` writes to a memory-backed directory (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` or
`/dev/shm`) at mode 0600, then zeroes and removes it when the command exits. It
falls back to the real temp dir only if neither is available, and says so on
stderr. Prefer `--as` when the tool will accept a value.

Dotenv values are taken literally to end of line: a trailing `# comment` is not
stripped from an unquoted value, because truncating a credential is worse than
keeping a stray comment. Quote the value to preserve it exactly.

The child's environment is readable through `/proc` by the same user, and a
child that dumps its environment dumps the secret. `--as-file` hands over a
path, so a tool that logs its arguments logs the path rather than the key.

## valetfs setup-claude

For a person to run, once, on their own machine. It merges these rules into the
user-scope Claude Code settings file (`$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json` if set,
otherwise `~/.claude/settings.json`), preserving every other key and its order,
with a confirmation prompt and a `.valetfs-backup` copy:

    "permissions": { "allow": [
      "Bash(valetfs exec *)",
      "Bash(valetfs ls *)",
      "Bash(valetfs status)"
    ] }

`--print` shows the JSON without writing. `--allow-cat` adds
`Bash(valetfs cat *)`, which hands whole secrets to the agent and is therefore
opt-in. Write and delete (`cp`, `mv`, `rm`) are deliberately absent: emptying a
vault should take a confirmation.

## Joining a session

A long base64url string with no explanation is a connection key; the user tapped
"Provision an agent" in the app.

    valetfs serve --join <KEY> \
      --grace 604800 \
      --resume-key-file "$HOME/.valetfs/e2ee.key" \
      > "$HOME/.valetfs/daemon.log" 2>&1 &

`--grace 604800` is 7 days. The default is 300 seconds, which unmounts and wipes
five minutes after the phone disconnects. The connection key is itself a bearer
secret: do not echo, log or commit it.

## Operational notes

- The vault is volatile on this machine. Daemon restart, a remote lock, or grace
  expiry clears it. Never delete a user's only on-disk copy unprompted.
- `mounted: false` with `used > 0` means unmounted but the heap survives. With
  `used == 0` a lock or grace expiry wiped it.
- No FUSE is normal. Without `/dev/fuse` the daemon serves over loopback WebDAV
  and the mountpoint stays empty; `backend: webdav` with `serving: true` is
  healthy. Reach files through the CLI, not the mount path.
- The CLI only reads `~/.valetfs/run/runtime.json`. `--runtime-dir` applies to
  `serve`. With two daemons, target one with `--daemon-addr=host:port`.
- `valetfs vault ...` manages a vault stored on *this* machine and defaults to a
  passphrase compiled into the public source. Always pass `--password-file` or
  `VALETFS_VAULT_PASSWORD`. This does not apply to `serve --join`.
- "Forget this daemon" in the app destroys the hub session, not just the local
  pairing. It is not a troubleshooting step.
